No Equilateral Triangles

LogicCoordinatesUnit Distance Problem
Game: Ten dots are each orange or red. Colour them so that no three dots of the same colour make a triangle with three equal sides.
How to play: Tap a dot to switch its colour. A triangle whose corners are all one colour is shaded blue. Can you make them all go away?

Look for the math

The answer is no: however the ten dots are coloured, some equilateral triangle has three corners of one colour. This is a small case of Ramsey theory: a big enough pattern cannot avoid having an ordered piece. It also shows that the plane cannot be split into two colours with no monochromatic equilateral triangle.

Fifteen triangles

Among the ten dots there are exactly 15 equilateral triangles, 9 with side 1 (6 pointing up, 3 down), 3 of side 2 and 3 tilted ones. The test found them from the distances and confirmed that the applet's list is the whole set.

Trying everything

With two colours there are 210 = 1,024 colourings. The test tried all of them: none avoids a monochromatic triangle, and the best have exactly one (60 of them do). The button above does the same, in the page.

Are dots 7 and 10 needed?

The proofs on the original page never use dots 7 and 10 (the last row's two ends), and ask whether they could be removed. They cannot. The test found a colouring of the other eight dots with no monochromatic triangle among them, and in fact removing any single dot leaves a colouring that works. So all ten dots are needed, even though the written proofs only mention eight.

Link to unit distances

Here every size of triangle counts. If only pairs 1 apart must differ, two colours fail at once (a triangle of side 1 needs three) and the Moser spindle shows that four are needed. Whether five, six or seven colours suffice for the whole plane is the open Hadwiger–Nelson problem.

Make a colouring with just one blue triangle. Then flip the dots one at a time. Can you ever reach zero?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
